questions.stem: Describe a mess.
options: A tangle of difficulties with no clear edge, such as 'things are not working in the branch'
A specific gap between what is happening and what should happen, written so you would know if it closed
A visible sign that something is wrong, such as a 40% rise in complaints over three months
A solution waiting to be approved by the owner before the team can start work on it
questions.why: You cannot solve a mess; you can only cut a problem out of it. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Describe a symptom.
options: The visible sign that something is wrong, such as 'complaints are up 40%'
The underlying cause of the trouble, which has to be found before anything can be fixed
A gap written so precisely that you would know the moment it closed
A tangle of difficulties with no clear edge that nobody in the branch can describe
questions.why: Real, measurable — and not the thing to fix. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Describe a problem as the chapter defines it.
options: A specific gap between what is happening and what should happen, written so you would know if it closed
Anything a manager complains about in a meeting, as long as it affects the results of the business in a measurable way
The first solution that comes to mind when a manager hears about a difficulty in the branch
A symptom with a number attached, such as 'complaints are up 40% since January'
questions.why: This is the only one you can work on. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Identify the test that tells you whether you are still holding a mess or a symptom.
options: Ask what evidence would show the problem is solved — if you cannot say, it is not yet a problem
Ask the boss whether the problem is worth working on and accept the answer without further questions
Count the complaints and compare the number with the other branches
Check the budget to see how much money is available to solve it
questions.why: If you cannot name the evidence of solution, you have a mess or a symptom. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Explain why treating symptoms makes problems come back.
options: The cause is untouched, so the visible sign returns
Symptoms are not real, so treating them wastes money without changing anything
Customers prefer symptoms, so they complain again once the symptom has gone
Symptoms cannot be measured, so nobody knows whether the treatment has worked
questions.why: Treating symptoms is why problems come back. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Describe what actually solved the elevator problem.
options: Mirrors in the lobbies — the wait stopped feeling long and complaints stopped
Faster motors, which cut the average wait from three minutes to under two
A new shaft and an extra lift, which the building owner paid for over five years
Fewer tenants, because the complaints stopped once several offices moved out
questions.why: Nothing about the lifts changed. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Explain the real lesson of the elevator case.
options: The frame decided which solutions were ever considered — the first frame ruled out the cheapest answer
Always install mirrors when customers complain about waiting, because the wait is mostly psychological
Engineers are useless on business problems because they only see mechanical causes
Tenants complain too much and managers should wait for complaints to fade before spending money
questions.why: The lesson is not 'install mirrors'. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify the frame that made mirrors visible as a solution.
options: 'Waiting feels unpleasant'
'The lifts are too slow'
'People wait too long for the lifts'
'The building is old'
questions.why: Each frame opens different solutions at different costs. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify the solutions the frame 'the lifts are too slow' allows.
options: Faster motors, a new shaft, better scheduling — costing millions
Mirrors and screens in the lobbies, costing a few thousand dirhams
Stagger start times and add express floors, costing little
Lower the rent to compensate tenants for the waiting
questions.why: An engineering frame gives engineering solutions. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify the four parts of a testable problem statement.
options: The gap, the evidence, the scope, the constraint
The cause, the solution, the budget, the owner
The mess, the symptom, the problem, the plan
The who, the why, the method and the deadline
questions.why: Miss one and the statement cannot be tested. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Describe the 'gap' part of a problem statement.
options: What is happening versus what should happen, in numbers — 'average wait 14 min; target 5'
Who and where the problem applies — 'front counter, Deira branch, peak hours only'
What cannot change while the problem is being solved — 'no extra staff before the fourth quarter'
How you know the problem exists, and since when — 'queue logs, January to April'
questions.why: Weak: 'service is poor'. Strong: 14 min vs target 5. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Describe the 'scope' part of a problem statement.
options: Who and where it applies — 'front counter, Deira, peak hours'
How you know, and since when — 'queue logs from January to April'
What cannot change — 'no extra staff before the fourth quarter'
The target number — 'average wait of five minutes or less'
questions.why: Weak scope: 'the company'. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Describe the 'constraint' part of a problem statement.
options: What cannot change — 'no extra staff before Q4'
The gap in numbers — 'average wait 14 minutes against a target of 5'
The evidence source — 'queue logs from three branches over four months'
The chosen solution — 'a queue-management app for the front counter'
questions.why: The constraint names what cannot change. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Explain what must be absent from a strong problem statement.
options: A solution — the moment 'we need an app' appears, framing has stopped
Numbers — they belong in the diagnosis and the analysis, not in the problem statement itself
Evidence — it should be collected after the problem has been agreed
A date — deadlines belong in the plan, not in the problem statement
questions.why: A strong problem statement contains no solution. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Describe the 'evidence' part of a problem statement.
options: How you know, and since when — 'queue logs, Jan–Apr, 3 branches'
The constraint on staff — 'no new hires before the fourth quarter'
The solution budget — 'up to 40,000 dirhams approved by the owner'
The owner's opinion — 'the owner believes the staff are too slow'
questions.why: Weak: none. Strong: queue logs with dates. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Describe an issue tree.
options: A way of breaking a big problem into branches, and branches into smaller ones, until each is something a person could investigate this week
A list of possible solutions arranged from the cheapest to the most expensive, so that the client can choose the one that fits the budget and the timetable
A chart of who reports to whom in the organisation, used to find the person responsible for the problem
A timeline of the project showing which part of the problem will be investigated in each week
questions.why: 'Sales are down' is too big; the tree cuts it. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Identify the two rules for an issue tree.
options: No gaps and no overlaps
Five branches and five levels
One cause and one effect
Big first and small last
questions.why: Branches must cover the whole problem above, and each item sits in one branch only. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Explain the 'no overlaps' rule.
options: An item must sit in one branch only, or you will count it twice
Every branch must have exactly five items so that the tree is balanced
Branches must overlap to be safe, so that nothing is missed
Overlaps make the tree bigger, which makes it harder to present
questions.why: Overlaps double-count. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Explain why students who make five branches at a level have usually gone wrong.
options: They have almost always overlapped the branches
Five is too few to cover a problem of any size
Trees need ten branches at each level to be complete
Five branches cost too much time to investigate in a week
questions.why: Two branches at each level is usually enough. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Identify the first branches in the chapter's restaurant example.
options: Fewer customers · customers spend less per visit
Bad food · bad service from the staff
New competitor nearby · an old menu
Prices too high · rent too high
questions.why: Revenue fell 18% → fewer customers or less spend per visit. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Identify the four questions used to size a branch.
options: How big is it? Can I get evidence? Could we change it? How fast could we know?
Who is to blame for it? How much will it cost to fix? Who approves the fix? When is it due?
Is it a mess? Is it a symptom? Is it a problem? Is it a plan?
Who is involved? What happened? Where did it happen? When did it start?
questions.why: Size the branches, then work on the biggest useful one. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Describe the rule for choosing the branch to start on.
options: Work first on the branch that is large, measurable and within your control
Start with the easiest branch so that the team has an early success
Start with the cheapest branch to investigate so that the budget lasts
Start with the boss's favourite branch so that the project has the support it needs to continue
questions.why: Large, measurable, within your control. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Explain why a branch you cannot measure is a problem.
options: It will stay an opinion forever
It is always the biggest branch in the tree
It costs the most to investigate properly
It must be the real cause of the problem
questions.why: A branch you cannot measure stays an opinion. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Explain what to do if no branch is large, measurable and controllable.
options: Say so plainly — that is a finding, not a failure
Choose one anyway, because the client expects a recommendation
Give up the project, because nothing useful can be done
Invent a measurement so that at least one branch qualifies
questions.why: Saying so plainly is a finding. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Explain why the exchange rate can be a cause and still be useless.
options: You cannot change it, so it fails the 'could we change it?' question
It is not measurable with the data available, so it stays an opinion in the report
It is too small to explain the gap on its own
It is a symptom rather than a cause of the problem
questions.why: A true cause outside your control does not help you. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Explain why framing is an exercise of power.
options: Whoever writes the frame decides what counts as the problem
Framing is done by the most senior person in the room, whatever the evidence says
Only consultants frame problems, because managers are too close to the work
Framing costs money, so the person who pays decides how it is done
questions.why: Framing is not neutral. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Explain what the frame 'staff motivation' rules out without saying so.
options: 'My supervision' as the cause
All possible solutions to the problem
Staff opinions about what is wrong
The budget for fixing the problem
questions.why: The manager's frame excludes the manager. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Identify the professional question to ask any client about their problem.
options: 'What makes you say that is the problem?'
'How much are you prepared to pay to fix it?'
'Which app or system would you like us to build?'
'Who in the team is responsible for this?'
questions.why: Ask it politely, and always. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Explain why the people closest to the work should be asked first.
options: They hold the evidence and are usually not asked
They decide the budget for solving the problem
They write the frame that the consultant works from
They own the company and will approve the solution
questions.why: Ask them first. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Explain what a brief that names the solution has done.
options: Ended the framing stage before it began
Saved time by skipping the parts of the project that add little
Proved the problem exists, because the client has already thought about it
Found the cause, because a solution implies a cause
questions.why: 'We need an app' ends framing. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Identify the kind of statement 'things are not working in the branch' is.
options: A mess
A symptom
A problem
A constraint
questions.why: No clear edge = a mess. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Identify the cost level of the 'waiting feels unpleasant' frame.
options: Very small
Millions of dirhams
Large
Unknown
questions.why: Mirrors and screens cost very little. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Classify 'our newest branch is failing' as said by the pharmacy owner.
options: A mess — no clear edge
A problem — a tested gap
A symptom with a number
A constraint
questions.why: The owner hands you a mess. See §2.1 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Classify 'sales are 30% below the other branches'.
options: A symptom — a measurable sign, not the thing to fix
A mess — a tangle of difficulties with no clear edge
A solution — the branch needs to raise its sales by 30%
A constraint — the branch cannot change its position relative to the others
questions.why: Real, measurable, and not the thing to fix. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Classify 'he wants a marketing campaign'.
options: A solution smuggled into the problem
A symptom — the owner's wish shows that something is wrong
A problem statement — it says what the owner wants to happen
Evidence — the owner's view is a source of information
questions.why: The owner has already chosen the solution. See §2.1 and §2.6.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's view when a manager says 'our staff are unmotivated'.
options: It may be the manager's or the system's problem — the frame decides what you investigate first
It is always the staff's problem, because motivation belongs to the individual and not to the system around them
It is never a problem, because motivation cannot be measured
It is a solution, because the manager has decided what needs to change
questions.why: Whose problem it is changes what you investigate. See §2.1 and §2.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a client who says 'we need a mobile app'. Determine what has been decided and ruled out.
options: The solution is decided and every non-app answer is ruled out without discussion
Nothing has been decided, because the client is only expressing a preference about the kind of solution
Only the budget is decided, because an app has a known cost
The problem has been framed well, because the client knows what is needed
questions.why: Five words that end framing. See §2.2 and §2.6.

questions.stem: Select the reframe of 'attendance at 8 a.m. lectures is poor' that opens the most new solutions.
options: 'Students do not see enough value in being there at 8 a.m.'
'We need an attendance app that texts students who are absent'
'Students are lazy and prefer to sleep late'
'The register is wrong and attendance is better than it looks'
questions.why: A wider frame admits more than one answer, like the elevator rows. See §2.2 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Analyse the frame 'people wait too long' for the lifts. Determine a solution it makes visible.
options: Stagger start times or add express floors
Faster motors in the existing lifts
Mirrors in the lobbies on every floor
Lower rent for tenants on the upper floors
questions.why: Each frame opens its own solutions. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's test for a good frame to take to a client.
options: Wide enough to admit more than one answer, narrow enough to be testable
As narrow as possible, so that the investigation is quick
As wide as possible, so that no cause is missed
The one the client already chose, so that the project has the client's full support from the start
questions.why: Wide enough and narrow enough. See Exercise 3 and §2.2.

questions.stem: Classify 'service is poor' as a gap statement.
options: Weak — no numbers, cannot be tested
Strong — short and clear enough for any manager to understand
Strong — it names the scope of the problem
Weak — it names a solution instead of a gap
questions.why: A gap needs what is vs what should be, in numbers. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Select the strongest problem statement.
options: 'Average prescription wait 22 min vs sister branches 9; till data, 11 months; new Ajman branch, all hours; no new staff this quarter'
'The branch is slow and needs a marketing campaign to bring back the customers it has lost to the clinic next door since it opened last spring'
'Customers are unhappy with the service at the new branch and have been complaining to the staff and the owner for several months'
'We need a pharmacy robot to speed up prescriptions at the new branch so that it can match the performance of the older branches'
questions.why: Gap, evidence, scope, constraint — and no solution. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Analyse the statement 'wait is 14 minutes; target 5; front counter, Deira, peak hours; no extra staff before Q4'. Determine the missing part.
options: Evidence — how you know and since when
The gap — what is happening versus what should happen
The scope — who and where the problem applies
The constraint — what cannot change
questions.why: Four parts: gap, evidence, scope, constraint. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Determine what to write when you lack evidence for a part of the statement.
options: The question you would ask, instead of guessing
A guess that sounds right, so that the statement is complete
Nothing — leave it blank so that the client fills it in
The solution, so that the client can see where the project is heading
questions.why: Write the question instead of guessing. See Exercise 1 and §2.3.

questions.stem: Classify 'we need an attendance app that texts absent students' as a problem statement.
options: Not a problem statement — it contains the solution
A strong statement, because it is specific about what will happen
A good gap, because it names what is missing
A good constraint, because it limits the solution to one option
questions.why: A strong statement contains no solution. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a tree whose first branches are 'fewer customers', 'lower prices' and 'fewer returning customers'. Determine the fault.
options: Overlap — returning customers already sit inside fewer customers
A gap — the tree does not cover customers who spend less per visit
Too few branches — a tree needs at least five at the first level
No fault — the three branches cover the problem completely
questions.why: An item must sit in one branch only. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a tree for 'revenue fell' with only the branch 'fewer customers'. Determine the fault.
options: A gap — customers spending less per visit is not covered
An overlap — fewer customers already includes lower spending
Too many branches at the first level for a problem of this size
No fault — fewer customers is the only possible cause of lower revenue
questions.why: Branches must cover the whole problem above them. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Select the testable bottom branch in the restaurant example.
options: 'Regulars who used to come weekly now come monthly — check the loyalty data'
'Revenue fell 18% over the last two quarters compared with the same period last year'
'Fewer customers are visiting the restaurant than before'
'The economy is bad and people are eating out less often'
questions.why: Testable = something a person could check this week. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Determine the depth of the pharmacy issue tree Exercise 2 asks for.
options: Three levels, checked for gaps and overlaps
One level, with the main causes listed side by side
Ten levels, so that nothing is missed
As many as possible in the time available
questions.why: Three levels deep. See Exercise 2 and §2.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a branch worth 2% of the gap. Determine the chapter's advice.
options: Not worth a week of your time — size it and move on
Start with it — it is easy and gives the team an early success
Investigate it first, because small causes are often the real ones
Report it as the cause, because it is the one you can prove
questions.why: A 2% branch is not worth a week. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Select the branch to start on: (a) big, measurable, controllable; (b) big, no data; (c) small, easy.
options: (a) — large, measurable and within your control
(b) — the biggest branch should always be investigated first
(c) — the fastest branch gives the team an early result
None — wait for more data before choosing any branch
questions.why: The rule names all three conditions. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Analyse 'the new clinic next door took our customers' as a branch. Determine why it may be abandoned even if true.
options: You cannot change the clinic — it fails 'could we actually change it?'
It is too small on its own to explain the fall in customers that the branch has seen
It cannot be measured, so it will stay an opinion
It is not a cause but a symptom of the branch's problems
questions.why: A true cause outside your control is useless to you. See §2.5 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine the branch the chapter prefers when two are equally big.
options: The one you can settle in days rather than months
The more expensive one, because it matters more to the client
The one the client likes, because the project needs support
The one with no data, because it has not been investigated before
questions.why: Prefer the branch you can settle fast. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Analyse the department head's brief for an attendance app. Determine what the frame ruled out.
options: Every reason for absence other than forgetting — timetable, teaching, value of the lecture
Nothing — the app would collect data on every reason for absence from every student in every class
Only the budget, because the app has a fixed cost
The students, because the app would be used by staff
questions.why: A brief that names the solution rules out the rest. See Exercise 3 and §2.6.

questions.stem: Determine how to raise with the pharmacy owner that his marketing campaign may be premature.
options: Ask politely 'what makes you say that is the problem?' and show the evidence sorted into mess, symptom and problem
Tell him plainly that he is wrong, because the evidence does not support a marketing problem of any kind and he should accept that
Run the campaign anyway, because the client has the right to choose
Refuse the project, because a client who has chosen the solution does not need a consultant
questions.why: The professional question, asked politely. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a project where the group simply agrees with the client's framing. Determine how the report is graded.
options: Poorly — the report is graded on judging whether it was the right problem, not on agreeing
Well — the client is always right about their own business and the consultant should follow
Neutral — the grade depends on the quality of the solution, not the frame
It depends on whether the solution works for the client
questions.why: Your first task is to establish whether it is the right problem. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Determine who should be asked first when diagnosing the pharmacy branch.
options: The staff closest to the work — they hold the evidence
The owner only, because he knows the business best
The marketing agency, because it has studied the market
The competitor, because it knows why customers moved
questions.why: The people closest to the work are usually not asked. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Analyse 'the building manager installed mirrors'. Determine which move of the five it shows done well.
options: Frame — a better frame found a cheaper solution
Decide — the cheapest option won the comparison
Diagnose — the lift motor was tested and found to be fine
Generate — many options were listed before one was chosen
questions.why: The frame decided which solutions were considered. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Analyse 'two pharmacists resigned in four months'. Determine what it is.
options: A symptom — a visible sign, possibly of the same underlying problem
The problem statement — two resignations is the gap to close
A constraint — the branch cannot hire replacements quickly
The solution — the branch simply needs to replace the two pharmacists quickly
questions.why: Resignations are a visible sign, not the gap itself. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Determine the constraint in the pharmacy exercise given 'you have two weeks and permission to speak to two staff'.
options: Two weeks and two staff interviews
No constraint — the exercise leaves the student free to choose
The marketing budget the owner has set aside
The clinic next door, which cannot be changed
questions.why: Constraints are what cannot change. See §2.3 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine the purpose of writing 'testable' at the bottom of a tree.
options: To reach something a person could investigate this week
To end the project with a clear conclusion
To impress the client with the depth of the analysis
To avoid having to collect evidence for the higher branches
questions.why: Branches end when they are investigable this week. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Classify the finding 'no branch is both large and within our control'.
options: A legitimate finding to report plainly
A failure of the group
A reason to invent data
A reason to pick the client's favourite
questions.why: That is a finding, not a failure. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Select the first task when a client hands you a problem.
options: Establish whether it is the right problem
Choose the solution the client has asked for
Price the solution so that the client can approve the budget
Agree with the client so that the project can start quickly
questions.why: Your first task is to test the frame. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a tree where 'new competitor' appears under both 'fewer new customers' and 'fewer returning customers'. Determine the fault.
options: Overlap — the same item sits in two branches and will be counted twice
A gap — the tree does not cover customers who spend less
Correct — competitors affect both new and returning customers
Too few levels — the tree should go deeper before naming any cause at all
questions.why: An item must sit in one branch only. See §2.4.
